content: 1. Comparators used in the studies include placebo or sham interventions, minimal or no intervention where the effect of the intervention can be isolated, and usual care as described in the trials, including care where the intervention effect can be isolated. 2. Critical outcomes for all adults include pain, back-specific function or disability, general function or disability, health-related quality of life, psychosocial function, social participation, self-efficacy, and adverse events as reported in trials. 3. For older adults aged 60 years and above, critical outcomes include pain, back-specific function or disability, general function or disability, health-related quality of life, psychosocial function, adverse events as reported in trials, changes in medication use, and falls. 4. No evidence synthesis was commissioned for all adults or older adults in the context of values and preferences. Judgments were made based on the experience of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members. 5. The WHO guideline on non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults includes an Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework summarizing the benefits and harms of multicomponent biopsychosocial care delivered by a single provider or a multidisciplinary team compared to placebo, no intervention, or usual care. 6. The benefits and harms of multicomponent biopsychosocial care for community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and above with chronic primary low back pain (with or without leg pain), were assessed in comparison to placebo, no intervention, or usual care. 7. Risk of bias was downgraded by two levels in studies due to unclear or serious risks related to random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants, clinicians, and outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, compliance, and co-interventions. 8. Imprecision was downgraded by one level for wide confidence intervals that encompass potential benefit and little to no effect. In some cases, imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to no events being reported or very wide confidence intervals that include potential harm, no effect, and potential benefit. 9. Minimal important differences were defined for specific scales, such as approximately 15 points on a 0 to 100 pain scale and 10% on the 0 to 24 Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RDQ) scale. 10. Despite some statistical heterogeneity (e.g., I-squared > 60%), inconsistency was not downgraded in cases where the direction of effect was consistent across studies or explained by subgroup analyses. 11. Studies included in the evidence base were conducted by various researchers, such as Jäckel (1990), Smeets (2006), Turner (1990), Abbasi (2012), Basler (1997), Bendix (1996), Lambeek (2010), Moix (2003), Morone (2011, 2012), Tavakian (2007, 2011), and Von Korff (2005). 12. In some cases, inconsistency was not assessed due to the inclusion of only one study for a specific outcome. 13. Small sample sizes led to imprecision being downgraded by one level in certain studies. 14. The WHO guideline emphasizes the importance of considering equity, human rights, acceptability, and feasibility in the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults, with judgments informed by GDG members' expertise. 15. The evidence synthesis highlights the need for careful interpretation of findings due to limitations such as risk of bias, imprecision, and heterogeneity in the included studies.
